chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub, from Abu Al-Sabbah who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a man who married a woman and found uterine horns in her. He (peace be upon him) said: 'She will not get pregnant, and her husband will not be able to copulate with her. He can return her to her family belittled, and there is no dower for her.'

I said, 'What if he had copulated with her?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'If he knew of that before he married her, meaning the copulation, then he copulated with her, so he was pleased with it. And if he did not know except after having copulated with her, then if he so desires afterwards, he keeps her, and if he so desires, he divorces her.'

key_terms.دَخَلَ بِهَا: Entered with her; refers to consummation of the marriage.
key_terms.صَاغِرَةً: Belittled/humbled; indicating the status of the woman when returned to her family.
key_terms.قَرْناً: Uterine horns; a specific physical defect in women affecting fertility and consummation.
key_terms.مَهْرَ: Dower/Mahr; the financial gift given to the wife in marriage.

ai.seo_question: What are the marital rights and options if a husband discovers his wife has a physical defect like uterine horns after marriage?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* elucidates the jurisprudence of *Gharar* (uncertainty) in marriage by addressing the specific defect of 'uterine horns' (*qarn*), which impedes both fertility and consummation. It establishes a critical legal distinction: if the husband was aware of the defect prior to marriage, he must return the wife without dower; however, if discovered post-consummation, he retains the discretion to either maintain the marriage or divorce her, reflecting the Shia emphasis on informed consent and the validity of the marital contract based on the actual state of the spouse.
